title: Technical Difficulties
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: Writing from the position of an Australian secondary teacher, this piece examines each category of educational technology—devices, digital platforms, and AI—through a single organizing question: does this tool serve learning? On devices, the author argues that the primary case against them is attentional: each notification interrupts cognitive processing for roughly seven seconds, and a device competes for student attention with an inherent advantage—it offers whatever students want. The claimed benefits of devices (digital literacy, research access, environmental benefit, personalization, accessibility) are examined and found mostly weak or double-edged, with accessibility for specific functional needs as the only persuasive case. On digital platforms, concerns center on gamification, easy AI-enabled bypass of written tasks, and the underestimated oversight burden they create for teachers who must verify digital submissions individually. On AI, the essay distinguishes harmful uses—student AI submission and AI-generated teacher lesson plans producing a cycle where nothing human needs to think—from genuinely promising ones, including flashcard-based spaced-repetition and AI marking of formative tasks with diagnostic output. Victoria, Australia has since announced device limits for primary schools from 2027, which the author welcomes as structural pressure to ask better questions.
points: The organizing question for any EdTech decision is not 'what can this tool do?' but 'does this tool serve learning, and can learning occur to the same degree without it?'

The primary case against devices in classrooms is attentional: each notification interrupts cognitive processing for approximately seven seconds, and the device competes for student attention with a competitive advantage—it offers whatever students want.

Devices and digital platforms that claim to personalize learning rarely close the achievement gap; most platforms lower the bar to ensure continued engagement rather than accurately diagnosing and remediating misconceptions.

The dangerous AI cycle in schools: AI-generated teacher lesson plans minimally connected to curriculum set student work that is also AI-completed—the only thing that needs to think is AI, and no learning occurs in between.

Genuinely promising AI applications include spaced-repetition flashcard algorithms (which personalize retrieval practice at a scale no teacher can match) and AI marking of formative tasks providing diagnostic data about what to teach next.
quotes: With any technology we use in education there needs to be one clear guiding question: How does this work in service of the learning?
Can the learning occur to the same degree without the technology? If it can, then why is the technology being used?
When every notification received by a student interrupts cognitive processing for roughly seven seconds you’re really just providing an invitation for students to display off-task behaviour.
When attention is the currency of learning, it is introducing a tool which actively competes with you for it and it is a fierce competitor.

Just because I can look something up, does not mean I’ll be able to understand it either. A teacher as an expert has countless ways to rephrase and reteach content to reach various points of need while also being a reputable source.

I’m yet to see a platform be able to accurately diagnose student challenges and adaptively address the misconception and build towards mastery. Many platforms simply lower the bar to ensure success and therefore continued engagement with the platform.

Furthermore if students are typing all of their notes, essays etc. They are then missing out on the cognitive friction caused by handwriting which causes us to process information slower, for longer and therefore lead it to be more likely to be retained.

what I have seen more of is clearly AI lesson plans which barely connect meaningfully to the curriculum which sets the students work which is then also completed with AI and we’ve created a cycle of learning where the only thing that needs to think is AI.

Does this task or tool service learning. Does this device improve or harm student outcomes? Maybe we don’t need a full ban on devices. We are not living in a luddite commune. But we should think carefully about when and why those screens come up.
